newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU seeks to play down French election fears.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks to play down French election fears.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers sought on Monday to play down fears that the sweeping election victory by French Socialists could delay the single currency and a new EU treaty.

At a meeting in Luxembourg to discuss the treaty, due to be agreed at an EU summit in Amsterdam in two weeks, ministers were generally cautious but said they saw no reason why Sunday's stunning triumph by the French left would disrupt plans.
"The realities of power will push things in the same direction as they have been," Germany Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told reporters.
"I think the economic austerity course will stay as far as the main points are concerned," he said. "(But) there will be nuances."
The French Socialists have said they are committed to economic and monetary union (EMU), but with conditions, including a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.

They want Italy and Spain to be in the first wave of countries to adopt the single currency from 1999 and have made clear they are unwilling to continue the fiscal austerity policy conducted by the outgoing government to qualify France for EMU.
New prime minister Lionel Jospin has also said he wants European policies to be refocused.

Although these comments -- and a crisis over proposed German accounting methods -- have led to renewed discussion of a delay in EMU and of a possible disruption of the treaty negotiations, most ministers were low key in their comments.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told Italian reporters the election of the Socialists was positive for Rome because of the Socialists views on Italy's EMU membership.
But, he said, it was too soon to tell what the Socialist win meant for Paris's European policy.
Most ministers said there was no reason that a new EU treaty could not still be agreed at Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 despite the French turnaround.
"We don't see any reason to make any change to any dot or comma because of the change of government in France," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country is EU president, said.
"(French) Socialist governments that we worked with in the past have been very European," he said.
Van Mierlo also dismissed concerns that Germany was using creative accounting techniques through the revaluation of its gold reserve to meet the EMU test.
"We will not be diverted by this discussion," he said.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook would not be drawn on the chances of a delay or a weakening of EMU criteria, saying only that because Britain was unlikely to join in the first wave, "It is for France and Germany to make up their mind."
"(But) we will not stand for any fudging," he added.
Cook did say, however, that while completing an EU treaty in Amstersdam remained the objective, his government would consider a delay if the issue was raised by others.
